questions.question_text:
Assertion (A): The $S_N2$ reaction of an optically active alkyl halide is accompanied by a complete inversion of configuration.
Reason (R): The nucleophile exclusively attacks the electrophilic carbon from the side opposite to the departing halogen atom.
options: A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
B) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

C) A is true but R is false.
D) A is false but R is true.
questions.answer: A) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Analytical Concepts

questions.question_text: Explain structurally why chloroacetic acid exhibits a significantly higher acidic strength than standard acetic acid in aqueous environments. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Chloroacetic acid has an electron-withdrawing chlorine group exhibiting a $-I$ effect. This structural feature stabilizes the resulting chloroacetate anion through charge dispersal, making it considerably more acidic than acetic acid.

questions.question_text: Define the term enantiomers in stereochemistry and state the primary structural condition necessary for a molecule to exhibit enantiomerism. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. The primary structural condition for enantiomerism is the presence of a chiral carbon center lacking any plane of symmetry.

questions.question_text: Identify and explain the specific structural difference between the pentose sugar molecules found in DNA and RNA backbones. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: The fundamental structural difference lies in their pentose sugars. DNA contains $\beta\text{-D-2-deoxyribose}$ lacking an oxygen at the $2'$ carbon, whereas RNA contains standard $\beta\text{-D-ribose}$ with a complete hydroxyl group.

questions.question_text: Justify chemically why isomeric primary aliphatic amines consistently possess higher boiling points than their tertiary amine counterparts. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Primary amines possess two hydrogen atoms attached directly to the nitrogen atom, allowing extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Tertiary amines lack these hydrogens, completely preventing hydrogen bonding, yielding lower boiling points.

questions.question_text: Describe a simple, single-step chemical test to definitively distinguish between phenol and an aliphatic alcohol like ethanol in the laboratory. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Phenol yields a characteristic violet coloration upon reaction with neutral $FeCl_3$ solution due to the formation of an iron complex. Aliphatic alcohols fail to react with $FeCl_3$, showing no color change.

questions.question_text: Formulate the complete balanced chemical equation and identify the intermediate for the Reimer-Tiemann reaction transforming phenol into salicylaldehyde. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, phenol reacts with chloroform ($CHCl_3$) and aqueous $NaOH$ at $340\text{ K}$, forming an intermediate. Subsequent acid hydrolysis yields salicylaldehyde ($2\text{-hydroxybenzaldehyde}$). The electrophile is dichlorocarbene ($:CCl_2$).

questions.question_text: Provide the balanced chemical equation and functional reagents for the Rosenmund reduction, explicitly detailing how over-reduction is prevented. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The Rosenmund reduction converts an acyl chloride to an aldehyde by hydrogenation over a palladium catalyst poisoned with barium sulfate. For example, acetyl chloride ($CH_3COCl$) yields acetaldehyde ($CH_3CHO$). The poison prevents over-reduction to alcohols.

questions.question_text: Detail how the Hinsberg test is structurally employed to chemically distinguish between primary and secondary amine species in the laboratory. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Hinsberg's reagent (benzenesulphonyl chloride) reacts with $1^\circ$ amines to form an alkali-soluble sulphonamide due to an acidic hydrogen. By contrast, $2^\circ$ amines form an alkali-insoluble $N,N$-dialkylsulphonamide, clearly distinguishing the two amine classes structurally.

questions.question_text: Define the concepts of a zwitterion and the isoelectric point in relation to the aqueous structural behavior of amino acids. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: A zwitterion is a dipolar, electrically neutral ion formed when an amino acid transfers a proton from its carboxyl group to its amino group. The isoelectric point is the exact pH where this neutral form perfectly dominates.

questions.question_text: Outline the three-step reagent pathway of the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis utilized strictly for preparing pure primary aliphatic amines. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Phthalimide reacts with ethanolic $KOH$ forming potassium phthalimide, which undergoes nucleophilic substitution with an alkyl halide. Subsequent alkaline hydrolysis releases a pure primary aliphatic amine. Aromatic primary amines cannot be synthesized this way.

questions.question_text: Contrast the $S_N1$ and $S_N2$ reaction mechanisms by strictly focusing on intermediate formation and resulting stereochemical configuration changes. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: $S_N1$ proceeds via a two-step mechanism forming a planar carbocation intermediate, leading to racemization. $S_N2$ is a concerted single-step backside attack resulting in complete structural inversion (Walden inversion) of the substrate stereocenter.

questions.question_text: Provide the balanced chemical equation for the iodoform test when applied to ethanol, identifying the color of the final precipitate. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Ethanol heated with iodine and aqueous $NaOH$ undergoes oxidation and subsequent halogenation. The reaction equation is $CH_3CH_2OH + 4I_2 + 6NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H_2O$, yielding a yellow iodoform precipitate.

questions.question_text: Read the following biochemical case context: A solution of sucrose is subjected to acidic hydrolysis in a polarimeter tube. Over time, the specific rotation of the solution shifts dramatically, leading to a phenomenon heavily monitored in food chemistry. Detail the specific rotation values before and after hydrolysis, explain the term 'inversion of cane sugar', and identify the two resulting monosaccharide units. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Sucrose ($\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$) is strongly dextrorotatory ($+66.5^\circ$). Upon acidic hydrolysis, it produces dextrorotatory $D\text{-glucose}$ ($+52.5^\circ$) and strongly levorotatory $D\text{-fructose}$ ($-92.4^\circ$). The net specific rotation changes from positive to negative. This optical phenomenon is called the inversion of cane sugar, yielding an invert sugar mixture.

questions.question_text: Read the following organic synthesis case context: An aldehyde lacking $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms undergoes a distinct disproportionation reaction when treated with a concentrated alkali solution (e.g., $50\% \text{ KOH}$). Contrast this behavior with an aldol condensation requirement and provide the balanced chemical equation for the Cannizzaro reaction of formaldehyde. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Aldehydes completely lacking $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms, like benzaldehyde or formaldehyde, undergo a self-oxidation-reduction (disproportionation) reaction when treated with concentrated alkali. For example, two molecules of formaldehyde ($HCHO$) react with concentrated $KOH$ to yield exactly one molecule of methanol ($CH_3OH$) and one of potassium formate ($HCOOK$).

sections.section_name: Section E - Long-Form Structural & Organic Synthesis

questions.question_text: Deconstruct the multi-step organic synthesis pathway required to convert benzene into pure phenol. Detail the specific reagents, intermediate chemical structures (including the diazonium salt formation), and thermal conditions strictly required for each successive step. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: The reaction sequence converts benzene to aniline and eventually phenol. Step one: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution with concentrated $HNO_3$ and $H_2SO_4$ to yield nitrobenzene. Step two: Nitrobenzene is reduced using $Sn/HCl$ to form aniline. Step three: Aniline reacts with $NaNO_2/HCl$ at $0\text{--}5^\circ\text{C}$ forming benzene diazonium chloride. Final step: Warming the diazonium salt with aqueous media yields pure phenol.

questions.question_text: Provide the comprehensive, three-step curved-arrow mechanism for the acid-catalyzed dehydration of ethanol to form ethene at precisely $443\text{ K}$. Identify the rate-determining step and state the structural fate of the highly reactive carbocation intermediate. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: The dehydration of ethanol to ethene at $443\text{ K}$ proceeds via three steps. Step one: Rapid protonation of the hydroxyl oxygen yields an oxonium ion. Step two: The slow, rate-determining cleavage of the $C\text{-}O$ bond generates a highly reactive primary ethyl carbocation. Step three: Elimination of a proton from the adjacent $\beta$-carbon structurally forms the $C=C$ double bond, yielding ethene.

questions.question_text: Analyze the four distinct structural hierarchies of protein folding. Define the precise chemical linkages or bonding forces responsible for stabilizing the primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary forms, explaining how simple linear polypeptide chains achieve final functional 3D complex architectures. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Proteins exhibit four structural folding hierarchies. Primary structure strictly defines the specific amino acid sequence linked by peptide bonds. Secondary structure involves localized folding into $\alpha$-helices or $\beta$-pleated sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure represents the overall 3D folding driven by disulfide linkages and hydrophobic interactions. Quaternary structure unites multiple folded polypeptide subunits into one functional protein complex.
